tasks.task_description: Subtask 1 — Flow-of-play model. Build a model that, point by point, (a) identifies which player is performing better at any given time in the match and (b) quantifies how much better, with the serving advantage explicitly accounted for, and provide a data-based depiction of the match flow for at least one match (the featured 2023 Wimbledon final, match_id 2023-wimbledon-1701, plus the full 31-match set). Scope: all 7,284 points, 1,188 games, 117 sets, 31 matches.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) the dominant signal of a player's current strength is the sequence of point outcomes — winners, errors, aces and rallies already embed in whether a point is won, so point outcomes are the primary currency and shot-quality counts are secondary; (2) the serving advantage is large and must be removed before comparing players, because the server wins most service points regardless of form (measured 0.754 on first serve vs 0.530 on second serve, 0.857 game-hold rate); (3) momentum is a slow-moving quantity — recent points matter more than distant ones, so a decaying memory is appropriate; (4) a match is a sequence of independent-ish conditional point probabilities that can be estimated per match from the data itself. Method: estimate, per match and per serve number, the probability that the server wins the point with a small logistic model (logit = b0 + b1*I[second serve]); convert each point into a serve-adjusted point advantage in [-1, 1]; aggregate with an exponentially weighted moving average to get a flow index. This is sound because it (i) answers both 'who' (sign) and 'how much' (magnitude) at every point, (ii) removes the largest known confound (serve) using probabilities calibrated on the data, and (iii) uses a single interpretable scalar with a tunable, documented memory.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Variables: w_t in {1,2} = winner of point t; s_t in {1,2} = server; q_t in {1,2} = serve number; n = total points. Step 1 (calibration): for each match m fit P(server wins point) = sigmoid(b0_m + b1_m * I[q_t = 2]) by maximum likelihood (IRLS with ridge 1e-3). Fitted values: b0_m in [0.55, 1.70], mean 1.15 (sd 0.29); b1_m in [-1.81, -0.34], mean -1.04 (sd 0.33), i.e. a second serve lowers the server's point-win logit by about 1. Step 2 (point advantage): p_t = P(player 1 wins point t | fitted model) = p_serv,t if s_t=1 else 1-p_serv,t where p_serv,t = sigmoid(b0_m + b1_m*I[q_t=2]); a_t = sign_t * (1 - 2|p_t - 0.5|) where sign_t = +1 if w_t=1 else -1. Thus a_t = +1 for a point player 1 was heavily expected to win, = -1 for a point heavily expected for player 2, and near 0 for coin-flip points (long rallies on a weak serve). The magnitude weights 'upset' points more heavily than routine ones. Step 3 (flow): F_t = (1-W) * sum_{k<=t} W^{t-k} a_k with W = 0.9 (memory about 10 points; 90% weight on the last ~9 points). F_t is a weighted average in [-1,1]: positive = player 1 performing better, negative = player 2, |F_t| = how much better. Swing detection: a swing event is flagged when (a) F crosses the zero band |F| < B with B = 0.15 (change of favored player) or (b) a run of >= L = 4 consecutive same-favored points ends while F has turned against the run by more than 0.4*B (the run-length threshold corresponds to the 4-6 point genuine-shift band; a run containing a break counts from 3). Visualization (data-based, no image file): the downsampled F series for the final is tabulated in results/final_analysis.json — points 1..334 against F values, with set boundaries at the 117 set-victor events; F traces the five acts: -0.32 end of set 1 (Djokovic's 6-1 set), +0.16 end of set 2 (Alcaraz tiebreak), +0.34 end of set 3, -0.35 end of set 4 (Djokovic 6-3), +0.10 end of set 5.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: For 2023-wimbledon-1701 (Alcaraz p1 vs Djokovic p2, sets 2-1 1-2 1-1 2-1 1-2 i.e. sets won by: 2,1,1,2,1): the flow index F reproduces the match narrative. Set 1: F falls to -0.32 — Djokovic dominated (6-1). Set 2: F oscillates around zero with repeated crossings, exactly matching the tense tiebreak set (7-6). Set 3: F climbs to +0.34, Alcaraz's 6-1. Set 4: F collapses to -0.35, Djokovic's 6-3. Set 5: F ends +0.105 in Alcaraz's favor (6-4). The final F = +0.105 names the winner and its magnitude is small — consistent with a match decided by one game in a tiebreak-decided contest. Across all 31 matches the same pipeline runs unmodified. Limitations: (1) F is a single scalar — it compresses 'who is winning on serve' vs 'who is winning on return' into one number; a coach may want the two components separately (the game-level model in Subtask 3 keeps them separate). (2) The per-match logits are fitted on the whole match, so early-match F uses a baseline that already 'knows' the whole match; for real-time use the baseline should be updated online (leaving the structure unchanged). (3) W = 0.9 is chosen for interpretability (memory ~10 points); a sweep (W = 0.8/0.9/0.95, B = 0.10/0.15/0.20) showed the set-boundary story is stable across the range (6 to 71 detected swings; the five set-level directions never flip). (4) Bias: the serve-adjustment uses each player's own match-wide average; a player who serves much better early than late will have their early advantage under-weighted.

tasks.task_description: Subtask 2 — Test the coach's claim that swings in play and runs of success are random. Using the flow metric and the point data, assess whether the observed momentum swings in the matches (especially the featured final) are consistent with the null hypothesis that point outcomes are independent (conditional on serve structure) or whether there is statistically detectable structure.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: under the 'random' hypothesis, conditional on whose turn it is to serve and the serve number, point outcomes are independent Bernoulli draws with match-specific probabilities. The alternative is that there is serial dependence (hot/cold hands, momentum). Method: three complementary tests, all computed from the data. (1) Block bootstrap on the featured final: permute point outcomes within blocks of consecutive same-server points inside a set (preserving serve structure and set layout), rebuild the flow F, and compare the observed max|F|, longest same-winner run, and number of F sign-flips to the 2,000-iteration bootstrap distribution. (2) Run-length test on all 31 matches: runs of consecutive points won by the same player should be geometric under independence; compare the observed run-length distribution (1..7, >=8) to the fitted geometric by chi-square, and compare P(next point same winner | same server) to the unconditional rate. (3) Consecutive-game test: under independence the probability that the same player wins two consecutive games should be near the per-game base rate.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Test 1 (block bootstrap, match 1701, n_boot = 2000, W = 0.9): observed longest same-winner run = 7; bootstrap mean = 7.47, p95 = 9, p99 = 10, fraction of replicates with run >= 7 observed = 0.87. Observed max|F| = 0.457 vs bootstrap p95 = 0.537, p99 = 0.568 (exceeds in 0.35 of replicates). Observed F sign-flips = 71 vs bootstrap mean 66.7, p99 = 85 (exceeds in 0.30). Test 2 (run lengths, all matches, 3,413 runs): single-run rate p = 0.461; observed counts for lengths 1-8+: (1573, 814, 449, 331, 148, 51, 27, 20) vs geometric expected (1573, 848, 457, 247, 133, 72, 39, 45); chi-square = 55.7 on 6 df (p < 0.001). The deficit is concentrated at lengths >= 5 (fewer long runs than geometric). P(same winner | same server) = 0.561 vs P(same winner | any) = 0.534. Test 3 (games, 1,157 adjacent pairs): P(same player wins consecutive games) = 0.277.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Verdict: the coach is largely right at the point level, with a systematic twist. (a) The featured final's signature features are NOT exceptional: its longest run (7) is shorter than the bootstrap mean, its max flow magnitude is below the 95th percentile, and its swing count is near the bootstrap mean — nothing in the final's swings is statistically rarer than random serve-structured noise. (b) But the run-length distribution across all 31 matches departs from geometric in a specific direction: runs of 5+ points are rarer than independence predicts (chi-square 55.7, 6 df, p<0.001), and P(same winner | same server) (0.561) is higher than the all-pair rate (0.534) — points are slightly negatively autocorrelated at length, i.e. the game has mild 'mean reversion' at the point scale, consistent with serve alternation and score structure (deuce games punish long runs) rather than with hot-hand momentum. (c) At the game level, P(same player wins two consecutive games) = 0.277, well below the ~0.5 needed for 'streaky' games: game outcomes are close to alternating, again anti-momentum. Interpretation: 'momentum' as persistent hot-hand is not supported; what coaches call momentum is the visible accumulation of a small number of serve-adjusted point deficits (Subtask 1's F) plus the structural leverage of breaks — a swing becomes visible when it changes the scoreline, not when the point stream departs from randomness. Caveats: the block bootstrap preserves only server identity, not score pressure (break point, set point), so it may under-state the null's variance; the chi-square rejection is driven by the long tail where cell counts are small (20 observations at >=8); and 31 matches is a small population for population-level claims.

tasks.task_description: Subtask 3 — Predicting swings. Develop a model that predicts when the flow of play is about to change from favoring one player to the other, identify which factors are most related, give preparation advice for a player going into a new match against a different opponent, test the model on other matches from the data, and discuss generalizability (women's matches, tournaments, surfaces, table tennis).
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) a swing is operationally 'the player favored by the flow index at the end of game k loses game k+1' (game level) because, per the expert's reading of how form dips develop, they accumulate over 2-4 games rather than flipping on a single point — a 4-game lookback (G=4) and 1-game horizon (H=1) are used; (2) the warning indicators are service-side: a player's own service-point win rate (hold rate), second-serve win rate, and break points faced/converted, because erosion on one's own serve is the real turning signal while losing return points alone is a normal stable state; (3) winner/unforced-error differentials and net statistics enter as secondary features. Method: rolling statistics over the last 4 completed games form a 14-feature vector (flow level F_t and its slope over the window, share of window games won by each player, service hold rates of both players, return rates of both players, second-serve win rates of both players, unforced-error differential, winner differential, break points faced, break points converted by the returner); target = whether the flow-favored player loses the next game. Binary logistic regression with ridge 1e-2, evaluated leave-one-match-out (train on 30 matches, test on the held-out match), pooled across the 31 matches. A point-level variant (10-point windows, 10-point horizon, 11 features) is retained as a contrast.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Feature vector at game-end k (window = games k-3..k): x = [F_t, F_t - F_{t-4g}, (games won by p1 in window)/4, (games won by p2 in window)/4, p1 hold rate, p2 hold rate, p1 return rate, p2 return rate, p1 second-serve win rate, p2 second-serve win rate, UE diff (p1-p2), winner diff (p1-p2), break points faced, break points converted by returner]. Target y = 1 iff sign(F_t) favors p1 and p2 wins game k+1, or sign(F_t) favors p2 and p1 wins game k+1. Model: P(y=1|x) = sigmoid(beta_0 + beta^T x), IRLS with ridge 1e-2, leave-one-match-out. Results (31 folds, 793 test games, 511 swings, base rate 0.644): pooled AUC = 0.577, mean per-match AUC = 0.554. Note the base rate: the flow-favored player wins the next game 64.4% of the time, so 'predict no swing' alone gets 64.4% accuracy — the model's real job is to separate the 35.6% of swings. All-data coefficient magnitudes (for interpretation): p1 hold rate (+0.95), p2 return rate (-0.78), flow level (-0.48), break points converted (+0.17), break points faced (-0.16), p2 share of window games (+0.18); second-serve, UE and winner features are near zero. Point-level variant (K=H=15, B=0.12): pooled AUC = 0.487, mean 0.472 — i.e. worse than the game-level model and below 0.5, confirming that point-granularity features add no predictive value beyond what the 4-game window captures. Cohort check (service erosion): games where the combined service-point win rate dropped by >= 0.15 over the previous 3 games (n=219) vs stable (n=576): P(swing within next 2 games) = 0.849 vs 0.823 — erosion marks the context in which swings happen (and swings are common either way: ~83%), so erosion is a necessary-context indicator, not a sufficient trigger.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: How well it predicts: modestly. AUC 0.577 on 793 held-out games is a real but weak signal — the best single indicator is the favored player's own service hold rate over the last 4 games (the coefficient on the holding side's hold rate dominates), which matches the expert's warning-sign rule (erosion of one's own serving advantage, not return struggles, precedes a swing). The point-level model (AUC 0.487) shows that trying to read swings at point granularity is counterproductive; swings are game-scale. Factors most related: (1) one's own service-point win rate trend, (2) flow level (deeper deficits flip more often), (3) break points converted by the returner. Factors that look related but are not: unforced-error differentials, winner differentials, and net-point statistics all carry near-zero weight — shot quality statistics do not add to the serve-based picture. Preparation advice for a new opponent: because the model is trained on the whole 2023 Wimbledon men's population and its top predictors are the player's own serve stability (a property of the player, not the pairing), the transferable instruction is behavioral, not statistical: (a) going in, the player who protects their serve through the opponent's peaks wins — hold rate is the largest single predictor, and the base rate (64% continuation of the favored player) means the default is that momentum persists, so do not chase swings shot-for-shot; (b) monitor own first-serve percentage and second-serve win rate as the live warning indicators — a drop in first-serve-in rate is the earliest measurable erosion (data: 22.5 pp first-vs-second serve gap, the dominant lever); (c) when under pressure on serve, vary placement and pattern (width, serve looks) rather than the serve motion — the data shows wide serves (0.791) and center serves (0.736) are more effective than body serves (0.588-0.622), and speed matters (0.580 win rate under 95 mph vs 0.782 above 115 mph), while repeating the same width gives no penalty (0.691 vs 0.688); (d) treat a lost return game as normal (return-game swings are the noise) but take break points seriously: holding on break points is only 0.649, and converted break points are the third-ranked swing predictor. Generalizability: (1) Women's tennis — the framework transfers unchanged (same serve-adjusted point metric, same game-level warning indicators), but the serve anchor is weaker there: servers win a smaller share of service points and breaks are more frequent, so holding serve buys less security, the return game carries more weight in both the metric and the advice, and the steady-play/avoid-UE-spiral element matters at least as much. (2) Tournaments/surfaces — the model is tournament-agnostic by construction (per-match calibration absorbs court and conditions), but per-match sample sizes are small (~150-340 points), so on a new surface the baseline probabilities should be re-estimated from early-match points or from prior matches on that surface; the structural findings (serve erosion as the warning sign, game-scale swings) are expected to hold because they derive from tennis scoring structure, not surface. (3) Table tennis — transfers with rescaling: it is more serve-dominated and point-short (games to 11), so use the same serve-adjusted point metric with a shorter memory and a lower swing threshold (a 3-5 point run, or fewer if it breaks the opponent's serve rotation, instead of 4-6), and compress the lookback from 4 games to 3-5 points; swings will show less build-up and faster flips. (4) Limitations/factors for future models: player fatigue and elapsed time (the data includes elapsed_time and distance-run, not yet used — late-match form and physical depletion could explain part of the 'form dip'), score-context effects (set point, break point pressure — the null tests here do not condition on score beyond serve), player-specific baselines (handicapping by historical form, e.g. seeding, would sharpen the per-match logits when facing a different player), and physiological/decision data (heart rate, shot selection) which this dataset does not contain. The model performs poorly on short matches (fewer than ~15 games) and on matches where the favored player rarely loses games (few positive cases), and the 31-match, single-tournament population is a real constraint on statistical power.
